Summarizing Datasets with `admiral_df`

Source: vignettes/articles/admiral_df.Rmd
admiral_df.Rmd

Introduction

While an ADaM dataset is being derived it is easy to lose track of what it contains: did derive_param_computed() add the parameter you expected, did a merge duplicate some records, is there still only one baseline record per subject and parameter?

admiral helps answer these questions with the admiral_df class. A dataset of this class can carry a little metadata about itself – its name, its ADaM class, and its key variables – and calling summary() on it prints a short report tailored to the kind of dataset it is, including some sanity checks.

This article shows how to:

  • tag a dataset with admiral_df() and read its metadata back,
  • use summary() to inspect a dataset in flight, i.e. at any point of a derivation pipeline,
  • keep the class and metadata when using dplyr and tidyr, as some common operations keep them, some keep them only in part, and some drop them.

Note: The admiral_df class and the functions described here are experimental, so their behavior may still change.

Required Packages

The examples in this article use the following packages and the example ADSL and ADLB datasets which come with admiral.

library(admiral)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(tibble)

adsl <- admiral_adsl
adlb <- admiral_adlb

What is an admiral_df?

An admiral_df is an ordinary data frame (usually a tibble) with an extra class. Everything you can do with a tibble you can still do with an admiral_df; it only changes how the dataset is printed and summarized.

All admiral functions which create or modify a dataset, such as the derive_*() functions, return an admiral_df. So as soon as a dataset has passed through an admiral function, summary() gives the admiral report rather than the base R one.

adsl <- derive_vars_dt(
  adsl,
  new_vars_prefix = "RFST",
  dtc = RFSTDTC
)

class(adsl)
#> [1] "admiral_df" "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"

In addition, a dataset can store three pieces of metadata:

Metadata Example Read back with
Name "ADLB" get_dataset_name()
ADaM class "BDS" get_dataset_class()
Key variables exprs(USUBJID, PARAMCD, AVISIT) get_dataset_keys()

The key variables are the variables which together should uniquely identify each record of the dataset. They are what summary() checks the record structure against.

Tagging a Dataset

The metadata is set with admiral_df(). Any data frame can be passed to it, whether or not it has the admiral_df class yet.

adlb <- admiral_df(
  adlb,
  dataset_name = "ADLB",
  dataset_class = "BDS",
  dataset_keys = exprs(STUDYID, USUBJID, PARAMCD, AVISIT)
)

When the metadata has been set, it is shown in a header line when the dataset is printed:

adlb %>%
  select(USUBJID, PARAMCD, AVISIT, AVAL) %>%
  head(3)
#> # An admiral dataset (name: ADLB, class: BDS, keys: STUDYID, USUBJID, PARAMCD, AVISIT)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   USUBJID     PARAMCD AVISIT                 AVAL
#>   <chr>       <chr>   <chr>                 <dbl>
#> 1 01-701-1015 ALT     Baseline                 27
#> 2 01-701-1015 ALT     Week 2                   41
#> 3 01-701-1015 ALT     POST-BASELINE MAXIMUM    41

and it can be read back with the get_*() functions:

get_dataset_name(adlb)
#> [1] "ADLB"
get_dataset_class(adlb)
#> [1] "BDS"
get_dataset_keys(adlb)
#> [[1]]
#> STUDYID
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> USUBJID
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> PARAMCD
#> 
#> [[4]]
#> AVISIT

get_dataset_keys() returns a list of symbols, so the keys can be passed straight to a by_vars argument of another function.

Updating the Metadata

Calling admiral_df() again on a dataset which already has metadata updates only the items which are supplied. Anything left as NULL is kept:

adlb <- admiral_df(adlb, dataset_keys = exprs(STUDYID, USUBJID, PARAMCD, ADT, DTYPE))

get_dataset_name(adlb)
#> [1] "ADLB"
get_dataset_keys(adlb)
#> [[1]]
#> STUDYID
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> USUBJID
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> PARAMCD
#> 
#> [[4]]
#> ADT
#> 
#> [[5]]
#> DTYPE

If one of the keys is not a variable of the dataset, perhaps because of a typo, a warning is issued and the keys are left as they were:

adlb_typo <- admiral_df(adlb, dataset_keys = exprs(USUBJID, PARAMDC))
#> Warning: Key variable `PARAMDC` is not in `dataset`, so no keys were set.
#> ℹ The keys set previously are kept: `STUDYID`, `USUBJID`, `PARAMCD`, `ADT`, and
#>   `DTYPE`.

To record that a dataset has no key variables at all, pass an empty list, exprs(). This is different from never setting the keys.

Where do the Keys Come From?

admiral never guesses the keys of a dataset. They can come from your dataset specification, from the by_vars of the derivation which created the dataset, or simply be written by hand. A specification usually provides them as a character vector, which chr2vars() converts. For example, with a metacore specification:

adlb <- admiral_df(
  adlb,
  dataset_keys = chr2vars(metacore::get_keys(spec, "ADLB")$variable),
  dataset_name = "ADLB"
)

The ADaM Class

The ADaM class decides what summary() reports. The supported classes are "ADSL", "BDS", "OCCDS", and "TTE", and for medical device data "ADDL", "MDBDS", "MDOCCDS", and "MDTTE".

Unlike the keys, the class does not have to be set: if it has not been, admiral infers it from the variables and records of the dataset. For example, a dataset with PARAMCD and AVAL is inferred as "BDS", and one with one record per subject as "ADSL":

get_dataset_class(adsl)
#> [1] "ADSL"

When printed, an inferred class is marked as such. If the inferred class is wrong for your dataset – for example an ADAE which has been restricted to device related events may be taken for device data – set it with admiral_df(). A class that has been set always takes precedence.

Summarizing a Dataset in Flight

Calling summary() on an admiral_df prints a report on the dataset. It always shows the name and ADaM class, the number of subjects, records and variables, and whether there is one record per key. Depending on the ADaM class it then adds:

  • ADSL: subjects per treatment arm, population flags, subject flow (randomized, treated, completed), treatment duration, end of study status, deaths and their causes, and age and sex.
  • BDS: per parameter the records, subjects, visits and the distribution of AVAL, the analysis visits, the derived records per DTYPE, and a check that there is at most one baseline record (ABLFL) per subject and parameter.
  • OCCDS: the number of distinct terms, treatment-emergent and serious records, records per severity or toxicity grade, and a check that each occurrence flag (AOCCFL, AOCCPFL, …) has at most one "Y" per group.
  • TTE: events and censored records per parameter.
summary(adsl)
#> ── adsl: ADSL summary ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Subjects (USUBJID): 306
#> Observations: 306 | Variables: 55
#> ℹ Structure: not checked, no keys set (see `admiral_df()`)
#> Subjects per treatment arm (TRT01P): Placebo: 86 | Screen Failure: 52 |
#> Xanomeline High Dose: 84 | Xanomeline Low Dose: 84
#> Populations: SAFFL 254
#> Subject flow: randomized 254 | treated 254 | completed 110
#> Treatment duration (TRTDURD, days): median 132 (range 1-212)
#> End of study (EOSSTT): COMPLETED: 110 | DISCONTINUED: 144 | NA: 52
#> Deaths (DTHFL): 3 (COMPLETED SUICIDE: 1 | MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION: 1 | SUDDEN
#> DEATH: 1)
#> Demographics: AGE median 77 (range 50-89) | SEX F: 179 | M: 127
summary(adlb)
#> ── ADLB: BDS summary ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Subjects (USUBJID): 11
#> Observations: 330 | Variables: 115
#> ✔ Structure: one record per STUDYID, USUBJID, PARAMCD, ADT, DTYPE
#> Parameters (3):
#>   PARAMCD  records  subjects  visits  missing   min  median    max
#>   ALT          110        11      18        0    10      23    129
#>   AST          110        11      18        0    16      24    168
#>   BILI         110        11      18        0  5.13    8.55  124.8
#> Analysis visits (AVISIT): Baseline, Week 2, Unscheduled 4.1, Unscheduled 4.2,
#> Week 4, Unscheduled 5.1, Unscheduled 6.1, Week 6, Week 8, Unscheduled 8.2, Week
#> 12, Week 16, Week 20, Week 24, Week 26, POST-BASELINE MINIMUM, POST-BASELINE
#> MAXIMUM, POST-BASELINE LAST
#> Derived records (DTYPE): LOV: 30 | MAXIMUM: 30 | MINIMUM: 30
#> ✔ Checks passed: at most one baseline record per USUBJID, PARAMCD, BASETYPE

Each item is only reported when the variables it needs are in the dataset. So summary() can be called at any point of a derivation: a dataset which is only half derived gives a shorter report, not an error. The checks report problems but never stop your program.

Checking the Record Structure

The structure line compares the records with the keys:

  • ✔ – there is one record per combination of the keys,
  • ✖ – some combinations have more than one record, and how many extra records there are,
  • ℹ – no keys have been set, so the structure was not checked,
  • ! – some keys are no longer variables of the dataset (e.g. after a select() or rename()), so the structure was not checked.

For example, imagine a merge accidentally duplicated some records. Without looking through the data, summary() reports it straight away:

adlb_dup <- bind_rows(adlb, slice(adlb, 1:2))

summary(adlb_dup)
#> ── ADLB: BDS summary ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Subjects (USUBJID): 11
#> Observations: 332 | Variables: 115
#> ✖ Structure: expected one record per STUDYID, USUBJID, PARAMCD, ADT, DTYPE,
#>   found 2 extra records
#> Parameters (3):
#>   PARAMCD  records  subjects  visits  missing   min  median    max
#>   ALT          112        11      18        0    10      23    129
#>   AST          110        11      18        0    16      24    168
#>   BILI         110        11      18        0  5.13    8.55  124.8
#> Analysis visits (AVISIT): Baseline, Week 2, Unscheduled 4.1, Unscheduled 4.2,
#> Week 4, Unscheduled 5.1, Unscheduled 6.1, Week 6, Week 8, Unscheduled 8.2, Week
#> 12, Week 16, Week 20, Week 24, Week 26, POST-BASELINE MINIMUM, POST-BASELINE
#> MAXIMUM, POST-BASELINE LAST
#> Derived records (DTYPE): LOV: 30 | MAXIMUM: 30 | MINIMUM: 30
#> ✖ 1 combination of USUBJID, PARAMCD, BASETYPE has more than one baseline record
#>   (`ABLFL`)

Comparing with ADSL

A dataset cannot tell by itself which subjects are missing from it. If ADSL is passed to the adsl argument, summary() also reports how many of the ADSL subjects have records – overall, in the safety population, and per treatment arm – and checks that every subject in the dataset is in ADSL. For an OCCDS dataset it also reports the subjects with a treatment-emergent record.

summary(adlb, adsl = adsl)
#> ── ADLB: BDS summary ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Subjects (USUBJID): 11
#> Observations: 330 | Variables: 115
#> ✔ Structure: one record per STUDYID, USUBJID, PARAMCD, ADT, DTYPE
#> Parameters (3):
#>   PARAMCD  records  subjects  visits  missing   min  median    max
#>   ALT          110        11      18        0    10      23    129
#>   AST          110        11      18        0    16      24    168
#>   BILI         110        11      18        0  5.13    8.55  124.8
#> Analysis visits (AVISIT): Baseline, Week 2, Unscheduled 4.1, Unscheduled 4.2,
#> Week 4, Unscheduled 5.1, Unscheduled 6.1, Week 6, Week 8, Unscheduled 8.2, Week
#> 12, Week 16, Week 20, Week 24, Week 26, POST-BASELINE MINIMUM, POST-BASELINE
#> MAXIMUM, POST-BASELINE LAST
#> Derived records (DTYPE): LOV: 30 | MAXIMUM: 30 | MINIMUM: 30
#> ✔ Checks passed: at most one baseline record per USUBJID, PARAMCD, BASETYPE
#> Subjects with records out of ADSL: 11 of 306 (3.6%) | safety population 11 of
#> 254 (4.3%)
#> Subjects with records per arm (TRT01A): Placebo: 5 of 86 | Screen Failure: 0 of
#> 52 | Xanomeline High Dose: 3 of 72 | Xanomeline Low Dose: 3 of 96
#> ✔ Checks passed: all subjects with records are in ADSL

A Worked Example

Summaries are most useful straight after a derivation, to confirm it did what you expected. Here we add a parameter for the ratio of ALT to AST and check the result:

adlb_ratio <- adlb %>%
  filter(is.na(DTYPE)) %>%
  derive_param_computed(
    by_vars = exprs(STUDYID, USUBJID, AVISIT, AVISITN, ADT),
    parameters = c("ALT", "AST"),
    set_values_to = exprs(
      AVAL = AVAL.ALT / AVAL.AST,
      PARAMCD = "ALTAST",
      PARAM = "ALT/AST Ratio"
    )
  )

summary(adlb_ratio)
#> ── ADLB: BDS summary ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Subjects (USUBJID): 11
#> Observations: 320 | Variables: 115
#> ✔ Structure: one record per STUDYID, USUBJID, PARAMCD, ADT, DTYPE
#> Parameters (4):
#>   PARAMCD  records  subjects  visits  missing     min  median    max
#>   ALT           80        11      15        0      10    22.5    129
#>   ALTAST        80        11      15        0  0.4444  0.8367      2
#>   AST           80        11      15        0      16      24    168
#>   BILI          80        11      15        0    5.13    8.55  124.8
#> Analysis visits (AVISIT): Baseline, Week 2, Unscheduled 4.1, Unscheduled 4.2,
#> Week 4, Unscheduled 5.1, Unscheduled 6.1, Week 6, Week 8, Unscheduled 8.2, Week
#> 12, Week 16, Week 20, Week 24, Week 26
#> ✔ Checks passed: at most one baseline record per USUBJID, PARAMCD, BASETYPE

The report shows the new ALTAST parameter with as many records and subjects as ALT and AST, so every visit with both values got a ratio.

Using the Summary Programmatically

summary() returns a list, which is printed. Its elements can be used in your own checks, e.g. to stop a program if the record structure is wrong:

smry <- summary(adlb_dup)

smry$structure$n_duplicates
#> [1] 2

What Happens to the Class and Metadata?

The class and metadata are stored as attributes of the data frame. Whether they survive an operation depends on whether it modifies the existing data frame or builds a new one. The table below summarizes what common operations do to an admiral_df with metadata set.

Operation Class Metadata Result
mutate(), filter(), arrange(), slice(), relocate(), head() kept kept Kept
mutate(.by = ), filter(.by = ) kept kept Kept
left_join() etc. and semi_join()/anti_join(), dataset as x kept kept Kept
bind_rows(), dataset as first argument; rbind() kept kept Kept
select(), rename(), transmute(), distinct(), count() kept kept, may be out of date Partially kept
group_by(), rowwise() dropped kept Partially kept
as_tibble(), as.data.frame() dropped kept Partially kept
group_by() … ungroup(), rowwise() … ungroup() dropped dropped Dropped
summarise(), reframe() dropped dropped Dropped
left_join() etc., dataset as y dropped dropped Dropped
bind_rows(), dataset not the first argument dropped dropped Dropped
tidyr::pivot_longer(), pivot_wider(), complete(), nest()/unnest() dropped dropped Dropped
admiral functions, e.g. derive_var_extreme_flag() kept not guaranteed Partially kept

Kept

Operations which change the values or the order of the records, but keep the data frame they were given, keep everything. This covers most of the code in a typical ADaM script:

adlb %>%
  filter(PARAMCD == "ALT") %>%
  mutate(AVALCAT1 = if_else(AVAL > 40, "> 40", "<= 40")) %>%
  get_dataset_name()
#> [1] "ADLB"

Joins and bind_rows() keep the attributes of the dataset which comes first. If the dataset with the metadata is the x of a join, or the first dataset of bind_rows(), everything is kept; otherwise the metadata of the other dataset is used, which usually means none.

# ADLB is `x`: kept
left_join(adlb, select(adsl, STUDYID, USUBJID, RFSTDT), by = c("STUDYID", "USUBJID")) %>%
  get_dataset_name()
#> [1] "ADLB"

# ADLB is `y`: dropped
left_join(select(adsl, STUDYID, USUBJID), adlb, by = c("STUDYID", "USUBJID")) %>%
  get_dataset_name()
#> NULL

Partially Kept

Metadata kept, but possibly out of date

select(), rename(), transmute(), distinct(), and count() keep the class and metadata, but they change the variables, so the stored keys may no longer match the dataset. The keys are stored as plain names, so they are not renamed along with the variables. summary() tells you when this has happened:

adlb %>%
  rename(SUBJECT = USUBJID) %>%
  summary()
#> ── ADLB: BDS summary ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Observations: 330 | Variables: 115
#> ! Structure: not checked, key USUBJID is not in the dataset
#> Parameters (3):
#>   PARAMCD  records  visits  missing   min  median    max
#>   ALT          110      18        0    10      23    129
#>   AST          110      18        0    16      24    168
#>   BILI         110      18        0  5.13    8.55  124.8
#> Analysis visits (AVISIT): Baseline, Week 2, Unscheduled 4.1, Unscheduled 4.2,
#> Week 4, Unscheduled 5.1, Unscheduled 6.1, Week 6, Week 8, Unscheduled 8.2, Week
#> 12, Week 16, Week 20, Week 24, Week 26, POST-BASELINE MINIMUM, POST-BASELINE
#> MAXIMUM, POST-BASELINE LAST
#> Derived records (DTYPE): LOV: 30 | MAXIMUM: 30 | MINIMUM: 30

Similarly, count() and distinct() return a dataset which keeps the name and class of the original, even though it is no longer an ADLB. Bear this in mind when printing or summarizing their results.

Metadata kept, class dropped

group_by() and rowwise() return a grouped data frame, and as_tibble() and as.data.frame() return a plain one. They keep the metadata, but not the admiral_df class, so print() and summary() fall back to their usual behavior. The metadata is still there, so calling admiral_df() without any other arguments restores the class together with it:

adlb_tbl <- as_tibble(adlb)

class(adlb_tbl)
#> [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"

adlb_tbl %>%
  admiral_df() %>%
  get_dataset_name()
#> [1] "ADLB"

{admiral} functions

All admiral functions return an admiral_df, so the class is always kept. The metadata, however, is not guaranteed to be: functions which build their result from a grouped or summarized dataset internally lose it, while others keep it. For example, derive_var_extreme_flag() drops it:

adlb %>%
  filter(is.na(DTYPE)) %>%
  derive_var_extreme_flag(
    by_vars = exprs(STUDYID, USUBJID, PARAMCD),
    order = exprs(ADT),
    new_var = LASTFL,
    mode = "last"
  ) %>%
  get_dataset_name()
#> NULL

Dropped

summarise(), the tidyr reshaping functions, and the grouped pipelines which end in ungroup() build a new data frame, which has neither the class nor the metadata. Note that group_by() followed by ungroup() drops everything, even though group_by() on its own keeps the metadata:

adlb %>%
  group_by(USUBJID, PARAMCD) %>%
  mutate(N_VISITS = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  class()
#> [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"

Where possible, use the .by argument instead, which keeps everything:

adlb %>%
  mutate(N_VISITS = n(), .by = c(USUBJID, PARAMCD)) %>%
  get_dataset_name()
#> [1] "ADLB"

Otherwise, call admiral_df() again with the metadata after the operation.

Recommendations

  • Tag the dataset late. As the metadata may be lost during a derivation, call admiral_df() once the dataset is (nearly) finished, or just before you want to summarize it, rather than at the start of the script.
  • Re-tag after operations which drop it. If you need the summary in the middle of a pipeline, call admiral_df() again with the metadata. Keeping the keys in a variable, e.g. adlb_keys <- exprs(STUDYID, USUBJID, PARAMCD, AVISIT), makes this easy.
  • Remove grouping first. admiral_df() does not accept grouped datasets, so call ungroup() before it.
  • Summarize after each important derivation. Comparing the summaries before and after a derivation is a quick way to see exactly what it added or changed.
  • Pass ADSL to summary() to see the subjects which have no records, or should not be in the dataset.
